title: MIRAGE: Metric Inference and Reliability-Aware Gaussian Estimation from Feed-Forward Vision

paper.title: MIRAGE: Metric Inference and Reliability-Aware Gaussian Estimation from Feed-Forward Vision
paper.abstract: Abstract Feed-forward 3D priors enable high-quality reconstruction from image streams but often lack reliable metric scale and suffer from long-term trajectory drift. In contrast, LiDAR–inertial estimation provides metrically accurate motion but lacks the image-space consistency needed for high-fidelity reconstruction. We propose MIRAGE , which anchors feed-forward visual geometry to LiDAR–IMU metric motion and regulates online pose corrections according to correspondence support and cross-modal agreement, jointly enabling accurate metric pose estimation and high-fidelity Gaussian reconstruction. Experiments on Oxford Spires, M2DGR and INS show that MIRAGE achieves accurate metric trajectory estimation, outperforming COLMAP, a widely used but computationally expensive reference for vision-only benchmarks. Motivated by the scarcity of long-horizon monocular benchmarks for large-scale indoor reconstruction, we further build a multimodal data-collection platform and use MIRAGE to establish accurate 6-DoF reference trajectories for a new vision-only benchmark. We benchmark recent monocular large-scale reconstruction methods on this dataset, providing a systematic evaluation of their performance in long-horizon indoor scenes.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Recent advances in 3D scene representation and camera pose estimation have substantially improved the quality and practicality of image-based reconstruction. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) ( Kerbl et al., 2023 ) represents scenes with optimizable anisotropic Gaussian primitives and an efficient differentiable rasterizer, enabling high-fidelity real-time novel-view synthesis. In parallel, feed-forward geometric models ( Leroy et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025a ; Wang et al., 2025b ) have made substantial progress in jointly inferring camera poses and scene geometry from unposed images. These advances have further driven the development of increasingly capable online tracking, mapping, and on-the-fly reconstruction systems ( Matsuki et al., 2024 ; Huang et al., 2024 ; Keetha et al., 2024 ; Meuleman et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2025 ) . More recent methods combine SLAM frameworks with data-driven feed-forward priors to further improve pose estimation and reconstruction quality in streaming scenarios ( Li et al., 2026b ; Ren et al., 2026 ) . However, purely visual reconstruction remains subject to global similarity ambiguity, while accumulated errors in learned geometry and pose estimation can lead to scale and motion drift over long sequences. These limitations highlight the need for an explicit metric anchor to achieve both high-fidelity reconstruction and a physically grounded trajectory. LiDAR–IMU sensing provides the metric scale and motion constraints missing from purely visual reconstruction. However, simply introducing a metric anchor does not resolve how feed-forward visual geometry should influence online pose refinement. Visual priors can improve local alignment and reconstruction quality, yet unreliable corrections may compromise metric consistency, while overly suppressing them can forfeit useful image-space refinement. Since the reliability of visual corrections varies with correspondence support and cross-modal agreement, a fixed fusion strategy is insufficient. The key challenge is therefore to selectively exploit feed-forward visual geometry while preserving a metrically consistent trajectory. We propose MIRAGE 1 1 1 The name reflects the gap between visual plausibility and metric consistency. , an on-the-fly reconstruction framework that combines feed-forward visual geometry with LiDAR–IMU sensing to jointly achieve metrically accurate pose estimation and high-fidelity Gaussian reconstruction. MIRAGE uses LiDAR–IMU motion as a metric anchor and selectively incorporates visual pose corrections according to correspondence support and cross-modal agreement, retaining useful visual refinement without compromising metric consistency. Given the stabilized metric trajectory, MIRAGE further leverages image residuals and LiDAR geometry for structure-aware Gaussian refinement, improving reconstruction quality while keeping the camera poses fixed. Experiments on Oxford Spires ( Tao et al., 2026 ) , M2DGR ( Yin et al., 2022 ) and INS ( Deng et al., 2025a ) demonstrate that MIRAGE achieves accurate and metrically consistent trajectory estimation while maintaining high-fidelity, photorealistic Gaussian reconstruction. Notably, MIRAGE achieves higher trajectory accuracy than COLMAP, despite COLMAP being a computationally expensive method widely used to establish reference trajectories for vision-only benchmarks. This demonstrates MIRAGE’s potential to provide reliable reference trajectories for benchmarking vision-only reconstruction methods. Long-horizon benchmarks for monocular reconstruction in large-scale indoor environments remain limited. To fill this gap, we develop a remotely operated capture platform with hardware-synchronized cameras, LiDAR, and IMU, and collect ten long-horizon sequences across diverse indoor scenes, as shown in Figure 1 . MIRAGE is then used to establish accurate 6-DoF reference trajectories for these sequences, forming a vision-only benchmark for large-scale indoor reconstruction. We further evaluate recent long-horizon monocular reconstruction methods on this benchmark. Our contributions are threefold: • Reliability-gated metric trajectory inference. We anchor feed-forward visual geometry to LiDAR–IMU metric motion and treat visual pose updates as correction proposals, selectively committing them according to correspondence support and cross-modal consistency to improve image-space alignment without compromising metric trajectory accuracy. • Pose-fixed structure-aware Gaussian refinement. We decouple scene refinement from trajectory estimation by fixing the metric camera poses and using image residuals together with LiDAR depth evidence to diagnose and repair oversized, misplaced, and missing primitives, improving geometric detail and appearance without perturbing the recovered trajectory. • A long-horizon benchmark dataset for real-world indoor reconstruction. We introduce a large-scale indoor benchmark comprising 10 synchronized RGB–LiDAR–IMU sequences, with 71,536 RGB frames spanning 59.6 minutes and 1.15 km across laboratories, dining areas, offices, and long corridors. The benchmark provides full 6-DoF reference trajectories and supports joint evaluation of long-horizon metric localization and high-fidelity 3D reconstruction.

sections.heading: 2.1 Visual Pose Estimation and Streaming Gaussian Reconstruction
sections.text: Learned geometry models ( Wang et al., 2024 ; Leroy et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025a ; Lin et al., 2025b ) provide dense priors for pose estimation and reconstruction. Recent methods incorporate these priors into visual tracking and global optimization ( Murai et al., 2025 ; Maggio et al., 2026 ; Maggio and Carlone, 2026 ) , exploit geometric context for reconstruction ( Chen et al., 2026 ; Xie et al., 2026 ) , or combine feed-forward predictions with global structure-from-motion optimization ( Deng et al., 2026 ; Pan et al., 2026 ) . Gaussian SLAM ( Matsuki et al., 2024 ; Huang et al., 2024 ; Keetha et al., 2024 ) extends 3DGS ( Kerbl et al., 2023 ) to incremental tracking and mapping. Other approaches predict Gaussians from image streams ( Chen et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2025 ) , optimize scenes incrementally ( Meuleman et al., 2025 ; Meuleman et al., 2026 ) , or combine learned priors with online pose and map optimization ( Lin et al., 2025a ; Li et al., 2026b ; Jiang et al., 2026 ; Ren et al., 2026 ) . Monocular reconstruction nevertheless remains scale-ambiguous, and learned priors do not guarantee metric accuracy or drift-free trajectories over long traversals.

sections.heading: 2.2 LiDAR–Inertial Estimation and Multimodal Gaussian Mapping
sections.text: LiDAR–inertial estimators ( Shan et al., 2020 ; Xu et al., 2022 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) recover metric motion from range and inertial constraints, while visual–LiDAR systems ( Shan et al., 2021 ; Lin and Zhang, 2022 ; Zheng et al., 2022 ; Zheng et al., 2025 ; Zhao et al., 2025 ) incorporate image observations. Multimodal Gaussian mapping ( Hong et al., 2024 ; Lang et al., 2025 ; Xie et al., 2025 ; Jiang et al., 2024 ; Deng et al., 2025b ; Cui et al., 2024 ) uses metric poses and LiDAR geometry for initialization and photometric refinement. Recent methods further incorporate Gaussian-map observations into localization ( Hong et al., 2025 ; Lang et al., 2026 ) or feed-forward priors into estimation and mapping ( Wang et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026a ) . MIRAGE regulates pose corrections using visual and geometric evidence to support both metric accuracy and rendering quality.

sections.heading: 2.3 Benchmarks for Multimodal Localization and Reconstruction
sections.text: Visual benchmarks ( Sturm et al., 2012 ; Dai et al., 2017 ; Knapitsch et al., 2017 ) support tracking or reconstruction evaluation without mobile 3D LiDAR streams. ScanNet++ ( Yeshwanth et al., 2023 ) combines high-resolution RGB, surveyed laser geometry, and mobile RGB-D/IMU data. Mobile datasets vary in sensing and supervision: MulRan ( Kim et al., 2020 ) lacks camera images, Hilti-Oxford ( Zhang et al., 2023 ) uses grayscale cameras, and FAST-LIVO2’s self-collected sequences ( Zheng et al., 2025 ) lack pose ground truth. RGB–LiDAR–IMU datasets ( Tao et al., 2026 ; Yin et al., 2022 ; Jiao et al., 2022 ; Wei et al., 2025 ; Zhao et al., 2024 ) cover diverse environments and platforms, while recent multimodal benchmarks ( Deng et al., 2025a ; Lang et al., 2026 ) provide reference geometry and poses for localization and rendering evaluation. Nevertheless, synchronized RGB–LiDAR–IMU benchmarks with full 6-DoF reference trajectories over long, object-rich indoor traversals remain scarce. Our extended captures in laboratories, offices, and dining spaces address this gap, supporting joint evaluation of trajectory accuracy and downstream Gaussian reconstruction.

sections.heading: 3.1 Overview
sections.text: Figure 2: Pipeline of MIRAGE. We anchor feed-forward visual geometry to LiDAR–IMU motion for metric pose estimation and streaming Gaussian mapping. Local metric constraints support visual pose refinement, while reliability-aware loop correction controls correction magnitude and selectively applies rotation to balance revisit alignment and local motion consistency. The resulting poses drive a triangle-associated Gaussian map. With poses fixed, offline geometry-aware refinement improves scene structure using image residuals and LiDAR support. Figure 2 summarizes MIRAGE. Given synchronized RGB, LiDAR, and IMU streams, we anchor feed-forward visual geometry to LiDAR–IMU motion for metric camera pose estimation. Correspondence support and cross-modal agreement regulate pose corrections (Section 3.2 ). The resulting poses drive streaming Gaussian reconstruction. After streaming, we fix camera poses and refine the Gaussian map offline, using image residuals and LiDAR depth to guide primitive splitting, replacement, and insertion (Section 3.3 ). We also introduce a synchronized multimodal indoor benchmark with MIRAGE-derived 6-DoF reference trajectories for evaluating long-horizon monocular reconstruction (Section 3.4 ).

sections.heading: 3.2 Pose Estimation
sections.text: We anchor visual pose estimation to LiDAR–IMU motion through a local-to-global pipeline. Tracking combines dense visual correspondences with LiDAR-derived metric depth to estimate frame-to-keyframe poses (Section 3.2.1 ). Local optimization refines keyframe poses using visual consistency constraints and metric position anchors (Section 3.2.2 ). Loop closure selectively corrects these anchors, and global trajectory fusion combines them with local visual motion to produce per-image camera poses (Section 3.2.3 ).

sections.heading: 3.2.3 Loop Closure and Global Trajectory Fusion
sections.text: We selectively update the metric camera anchors through observation-supported loop correction and combine them with the locally refined visual trajectory through metric-anchored visual motion fusion to obtain per-image camera poses. Observation-supported loop correction. We generate initial loop candidates following ( Liu et al., 2026 ) and rigidly align the resulting pose-graph optimization (PGO) proposals to the current metric trajectory without scale fitting. We assess each proposal from two complementary perspectives: (1) geometric consistency , evaluating improvements in revisit alignment and the risk of disrupting local structure; and (2) visual consistency , evaluating reprojection agreement with available image correspondences. These cues determine the accepted correction magnitude. Rotation updates are gated separately and require additional geometric benefit relative to their risk; otherwise, the current metric orientations are retained, as shown in Figure 2 . Accepted corrections update the metric anchors and propagate to subsequent metric poses. Details are provided in Appendix A.2.3 . Metric-anchored visual motion fusion. We interpolate consecutive metric anchors to obtain a baseline camera trajectory. We then incorporate visual motion between these anchors, using the deviation of the visual trajectory from the interpolation of its poses at the same two anchor timestamps. Let 𝐓 M ​ ( t ) \mathbf{T}^{\mathrm{M}}(t) interpolate the accepted metric anchors, 𝐓 V ​ ( t ) \mathbf{T}^{\mathrm{V}}(t) denote the locally refined visual trajectory, and 𝐓 ¯ V ​ ( t ) \overline{\mathbf{T}}^{\mathrm{V}}(t) interpolate the visual poses at the same two anchor timestamps. We obtain the fused camera pose 𝐓 F ​ ( t ) \mathbf{T}^{\mathrm{F}}(t) by combining their rotation and position components: 𝐓 F ​ ( t ) = ( 𝐑 M ​ ( t ) ​ 𝐑 ¯ V ​ ( t ) ⊤ ​ 𝐑 V ​ ( t ) , 𝐩 M ​ ( t ) + 𝐩 V ​ ( t ) − 𝐩 ¯ V ​ ( t ) ) . \mathbf{T}^{\mathrm{F}}(t)=\left(\mathbf{R}^{\mathrm{M}}(t)\overline{\mathbf{R}}^{\mathrm{V}}(t)^{\top}\mathbf{R}^{\mathrm{V}}(t),\;\mathbf{p}^{\mathrm{M}}(t)+\mathbf{p}^{\mathrm{V}}(t)-\overline{\mathbf{p}}^{\mathrm{V}}(t)\right). (2) The fused trajectory matches the metric anchors exactly while retaining visual motion residuals between them. Details are provided in Appendix A.2.4 . We optionally refine the accepted metric trajectory offline using hierarchical LiDAR bundle adjustment ( Liu et al., 2023 ) , exporting a separate trajectory as described in Appendix A.2.5 .

sections.heading: 3.3 Geometry-Aware Gaussian Reconstruction
sections.text: We reconstruct scenes using LiDAR to constrain geometry and RGB images to supervise appearance. Inspired by PLANING ( Jiang et al., 2026 ) , we use a triangle–Gaussian representation that couples explicit surface geometry with Gaussian appearance. Streaming Gaussian reconstruction. For each incoming keyframe, we initialize triangle geometry from LiDAR depth and normals, and Gaussian appearance from RGB observations. We then jointly optimize geometry and appearance through differentiable rendering: depth and normal consistency constrain geometry, while photometric losses supervise appearance. When camera poses are updated, we transform the associated primitives accordingly to maintain map consistency. Details are provided in Appendix A.3 . Geometry-aware Gaussian refinement. Following prior work ( Li et al., 2026b ; Meuleman et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) , we refine the streamed scene offline to improve global scene consistency and reconstruction accuracy. With camera poses fixed, LiDAR depth constrains geometry, while RGB images refine appearance. During refinement, we periodically diagnose and repair regions with high rendering error using motion-compensated LiDAR depth and multi-view consistency checks. (1) Oversized Gaussians whose depths agree with LiDAR measurements but fail to resolve image detail are split into smaller primitives. (2) Gaussians with persistent depth disagreement are replaced with primitives reinitialized using LiDAR depth and local normals. (3) At locations with valid LiDAR depth but insufficient Gaussian coverage, we insert new primitives using depth for position, local normals for orientation, and RGB observations for color. Alongside the photometric loss, we apply a point-to-plane penalty constructed from LiDAR depth and local normals to newly created or reinitialized Gaussians, penalizing position errors along the normal direction while allowing tangential adjustment. Repair criteria and loss details are provided in Appendix A.3.2 .

sections.heading: 3.4 A Benchmark for Long-Horizon Indoor Reconstruction
sections.text: We introduce a benchmark for long-horizon monocular streaming reconstruction. Our platform (Fig. 1 , right) integrates a wide-angle RGB camera, two LiDARs, and one LiDAR’s built-in IMU. The dual-LiDAR configuration combines broad coverage for robust localization with dense sampling for detailed reconstruction. Custom hardware synchronization and calibrated extrinsics align the sensor streams. We collected sequences through low-speed teleoperation to limit motion blur and removed blurred images through manual inspection. The dataset comprises 10 sequences across four categories: laboratories and dining areas with numerous objects and reflective surfaces, an office, and long, low-texture corridors that challenge visual tracking. It contains 71,536 RGB images at 2880 × 1860 2880\times 1860 resolution, spanning 59.6 minutes and 1.15 km, with trajectories approaching 200 m. We provide synchronized RGB–LiDAR–IMU data, sensor intrinsics and extrinsics, global LiDAR reference point clouds, and MIRAGE-derived 6-DoF reference poses. MIRAGE’s trajectory accuracy is validated on Oxford Spires ( Tao et al., 2026 ) and M2DGR ( Yin et al., 2022 ) . Platform details and dataset statistics appear in Appendix A.4 . We evaluate RGB-only methods on global trajectory accuracy and downstream reconstruction quality. We report absolute trajectory error (ATE) RMSE after Sim(3) alignment to the reference poses. For reconstruction evaluation, we train standard 3DGS ( Kerbl et al., 2023 ) with each method’s predicted poses held fixed. Held-out novel view synthesis (NVS) PSNR serves as a downstream indicator of local multi-view pose consistency.

sections.heading: 4.1 Experimental Setup
sections.text: Datasets and Metrics. We evaluate MIRAGE on Oxford Spires ( Tao et al., 2026 ) , M2DGR ( Yin et al., 2022 ) , and INS ( Deng et al., 2025a ) , reporting absolute trajectory error (ATE) RMSE for trajectory accuracy and PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS ( Zhang et al., 2018 ) for rendering quality. We additionally evaluate representative vision-only methods on our proposed MIRAGE benchmark, reporting ATE RMSE after Sim(3) alignment to the reference trajectories we provide. Details are provided in Appendix A.5 . Baselines. On Oxford Spires, M2DGR, and INS, our comparisons include LiDAR–inertial odometry (EllipseLIO ( Border and Chli, 2026 ) ), LiDAR–inertial–visual odometry (Fast-LIVO2 ( Zheng et al., 2025 ) ), LiDAR–inertial SLAM without visual input (Fast-LIO-SLAM and Voxel-SLAM ( Liu et al., 2026 ) ), and vision-only methods (LingBot-Map ( Chen et al., 2026 ) , GLUEMAP ( Pan et al., 2026 ) , and COLMAP ( Schönberger and Frahm, 2016 ) ). We also compare with Gaussian-LIC2 ( Lang et al., 2026 ) , a tightly coupled LiDAR–inertial–visual Gaussian SLAM system. On our MIRAGE benchmark, we evaluate recent strong vision-only methods, including LingBot-Map, GLUEMAP, LoGeR ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) , Scal3R ( Xie et al., 2026 ) , and ABot-Recon ( Han et al., 2026 ) , alongside MASt3R-SLAM ( Murai et al., 2025 ) . Implementation Details. Following the 3DGS evaluation protocol ( Kerbl et al., 2023 ) , we hold out every eighth image for rendering evaluation. LiDAR–inertial local bundle adjustment uses a ten-scan sliding window. Gaussian refinement runs for 15,000 steps with camera poses and exposure transforms fixed, performing splitting every 1,000 steps from step 2,000 through 8,000. All experiments are conducted on NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPUs.

sections.heading: 4.2 Trajectory Accuracy

Averaged equally across sequences, its ATE is 4.22 cm versus 7.49 cm for EllipseLIO, a 43.7% reduction. On large-scale Oxford Spires traversals and low-texture INS scenes, LingBot-Map exhibits substantial trajectory errors, while Fast-LIVO2 and Gaussian-LIC2 show severe errors or failures in our reproductions. MIRAGE maintains ATE below 10 cm on every sequence. These results are consistent with its reliability-aware design: metric anchors constrain drift, while correspondence support and cross-modal agreement regulate visual corrections to exploit useful evidence and limit unreliable updates. sections.heading: 4.3 Rendering Quality
sections.text: We compare MIRAGE with Gaussian-LIC2 and offline 3DGS trained from scratch using MIRAGE trajectories (Table 2 ). We evaluate 12 sequences, excluding three for which Gaussian-LIC2 did not complete reconstruction. MIRAGE achieves higher PSNR than Gaussian-LIC2 on 10 of 12 sequences, with a mean gain of 3.27 dB. Using identical camera trajectories, our refined streaming maps also exceed offline 3DGS by 1.15 dB in mean PSNR. These results are consistent with the complementary benefits of reliable multi-view alignment and Gaussian refinement that combines LiDAR-guided structural repair with RGB appearance supervision to recover scene detail. sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We presented MIRAGE, which anchors feed-forward visual priors to LiDAR–IMU motion for metric pose estimation and Gaussian reconstruction. Visual and geometric evidence guide trajectory corrections, while LiDAR depth and image residuals drive Gaussian repair with camera poses fixed. Experiments on Oxford Spires, M2DGR, and INS demonstrate accurate trajectories and high-fidelity rendering. Our synchronized multimodal benchmark comprises 10 sequences across four indoor scene categories, with 71,536 RGB images spanning 59.6 minutes and 1.15 km. With MIRAGE-derived 6-DoF reference trajectories, sensor calibration, and global LiDAR maps, the benchmark provides the community with a common testbed for evaluating trajectory accuracy and downstream novel-view synthesis in monocular streaming reconstruction, supporting further advances in long-horizon indoor reconstruction.

sections.text: We obtain initial loop candidates and PGO proposals following ( Liu et al., 2026 ) . Figure 4 summarizes candidate selection using available observations. Supported visual reprojection evidence is checked first. If no candidate is selected, geometric gains must outweigh disagreement across observation subsets and local degradation risk, with visual corroboration where available. Both branches favor translation-only corrections; rotation requires additional geometric benefit relative to its risk. Accepted corrections update the supported anchors and propagate to subsequent metric poses; rejection preserves the current accepted trajectory.

sections.heading: A.2.4 Metric-Anchored Visual Motion Fusion
sections.text: We apply Equation 2 between consecutive accepted metric anchors with visual support, using the following interpolation and update rules: (1) Interpolation. Metric anchors and visual endpoint poses are interpolated at the same sensor timestamps using linear position interpolation and shortest-arc quaternion SLERP. An interval is fused only after both anchor estimates become available. (2) Anchor updates. Accepted loop corrections trigger recomputation of the affected fused poses using the updated anchors and the stored visual trajectory. The visual translation residual remains in world coordinates, while the visual rotation residual is composed with the interpolated metric orientation. (3) Boundary handling. Before the right anchor becomes available, poses follow available LiDAR–IMU odometry relative to the latest accepted anchor and are revised upon finalization. A camera-only tail at sequence end follows visual relative motion from the last supported fused pose. Startup frames without metric support retain their initial pose estimates.

sections.heading: A.2.5 Optional Offline Hierarchical Pose Refinement
sections.text: After streaming and loop correction, we initialize hierarchical LiDAR bundle adjustment ( Liu et al., 2023 ) from the accepted camera trajectory, converted to scan-time IMU poses using calibrated extrinsics and coordinate transforms. Hierarchical optimization refines LiDAR alignment within and across submaps, and the resulting pose increments are transferred back to camera timestamps.

sections.heading: A.3.1 Streaming Gaussian Reconstruction
sections.text: Representation and initialization. Following ( Jiang et al., 2026 ) , each triangle carries learnable vertices, opacity, and appearance features, and supports differentiable depth and normal rendering. Associated Gaussians model appearance, with their centers parameterized by the triangle barycenter plus learnable 3D offsets. For each mapping keyframe, positive differences between observed and rendered Laplacian-of-Gaussian responses identify unresolved image detail, while depth-adaptive spatial filtering suppresses redundant primitives. LiDAR-derived depth and normals initialize triangle positions and orientations. Associated Gaussians start at the triangle barycenter, with appearance initialized from RGB observations. Rendering losses. With camera poses fixed during each mapping update, we jointly optimize geometry and appearance using ℒ stream \displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{stream}} = ℒ photo + λ d ​ ‖ D ^ T − D ‖ 1 + λ n ​ ‖ 𝐍 ^ T − 𝐍 ‖ 1 \displaystyle=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{photo}}+\lambda_{d}\left\|\widehat{D}^{\mathrm{T}}-D\right\|_{1}+\lambda_{n}\left\|\widehat{\mathbf{N}}^{\mathrm{T}}-\mathbf{N}\right\|_{1} (9) + λ inv ​ ‖ ( D ^ G ) − 1 − D − 1 ‖ 1 + λ o ​ ℒ opacity , \displaystyle+\lambda_{\mathrm{inv}}\left\|(\widehat{D}^{\mathrm{G}})^{-1}-D^{-1}\right\|_{1}+\lambda_{o}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{opacity}}, ℒ photo \displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{photo}} = ( 1 − λ s ) ​ ‖ 𝐈 ^ G − 𝐈 ‖ 1 + λ s ​ [ 1 − SSIM ⁡ ( 𝐈 ^ G , 𝐈 ) ] . \displaystyle=(1-\lambda_{s})\left\|\widehat{\mathbf{I}}^{\mathrm{G}}-\mathbf{I}\right\|_{1}+\lambda_{s}\left[1-\operatorname{SSIM}(\widehat{\mathbf{I}}^{\mathrm{G}},\mathbf{I})\right]. Here, 𝐈 \mathbf{I} is the observed RGB image, and D , 𝐍 D,\mathbf{N} are LiDAR-derived depth and normal targets. Superscripts T \mathrm{T} and G \mathrm{G} denote triangle and Gaussian renderings, respectively. The norms denote mean absolute errors over valid pixels, and ℒ opacity \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{opacity}} regularizes triangle opacity following ( Jiang et al., 2026 ) . Depth and normal losses constrain triangle geometry, inverse-depth supervision constrains Gaussian placement, and photometric supervision refines appearance while also updating geometry through the triangle–Gaussian association. The λ \lambda coefficients balance these terms. Pose updates. When a source-keyframe pose changes, we apply its rigid correction to the associated triangle vertices and Gaussian centers, rotating Gaussian offsets and orientations accordingly. This keeps the map consistent with the corrected camera trajectory. CPU–GPU memory management. To reduce GPU memory usage as the scene grows, we offload inactive primitives and their optimizer states to CPU memory and reload them when their source keyframes become relevant. Triangle–Gaussian associations and optimizer states are preserved across transfers, allowing optimization to resume without reinitialization. Pose corrections update both CPU- and GPU-resident primitives to maintain consistency throughout the map.

sections.heading: A.4.1 Sensor Suite and Robot Platform
sections.text: Our data collection platform (Figure 5 ) integrates an industrial RGB camera ( SENSING TRD1-G2A GMSL2 ), two Livox MID-360 LiDARs with built-in IMUs, and an onboard computer. Mounted on an AgileX mobile robot, the platform supports teleoperated data collection and online scene reconstruction. Each LiDAR has a horizontal field of view (FoV) of 360 ∘ 360^{\circ} and a vertical FoV of − 7 ∘ -7^{\circ} to 52 ∘ 52^{\circ} . Following RISED ( Jiang et al., 2025 ) , we mount one LiDAR horizontally and the other at an incline to broaden spatial coverage while avoiding mutual occlusion. The horizontal LiDAR captures distant structures to constrain pose estimation, while the inclined LiDAR densely samples nearby surfaces for detailed mapping. Inertial measurements are provided by the horizontal LiDAR’s built-in IMU. The camera is connected to an NVIDIA Thor device. It captures images at a resolution of 2880 × 1860 2880\times 1860 pixels, with a horizontal FoV of 64 ∘ 64^{\circ} , a vertical FoV of 40 ∘ 40^{\circ} , and an acquisition rate of 20 ​ Hz 20\,\mathrm{Hz} . Images and their associated timestamps are streamed from Thor to an onboard industrial computer through ZeroMQ. The industrial computer is equipped with an NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU for SLAM and scene reconstruction.

sections.heading: A.4.2 Calibration and Time Synchronization
sections.text: We estimate the inter-LiDAR extrinsics using GICP ( Chen et al., 2022 ) . Initialized from the assembly drawings, a shared rigid transform is jointly refined using point clouds collected in five distinct scenes with the platform stationary. LiDAR–camera extrinsics are estimated using FAST-Calib ( Zheng and Zhang, 2026 ) . We acquire paired images and LiDAR recordings of a calibration target at multiple positions, orientations, and distances to provide complementary geometric constraints. We qualitatively validate the estimated extrinsics by projecting RGB colors onto the LiDAR point cloud and visually inspecting the colorization for misalignment artifacts. Time synchronization combines Precision Time Protocol (PTP) clock synchronization with external camera triggering. A Xingqi XQ500 synchronization unit provides the common time reference and camera trigger signals. The LiDAR clocks synchronize to the PTP reference over Ethernet. Each image is timestamped with its corresponding camera trigger time. We verify image timestamps by imaging a reference clock display and comparing the displayed times with the recorded timestamps, with observed discrepancies below 10 ​ ms 10\,\mathrm{ms} .

sections.heading: A.4.3 Collection Protocol and Dataset Statistics
sections.text: Our dataset comprises 10 sequences across four indoor scene categories: laboratories, dining areas, an office, and long corridors. Laboratories and dining areas contain numerous objects and reflective surfaces, challenging detailed geometry recovery and appearance modeling. Long, low-texture corridors challenge visual tracking and long-term trajectory consistency. We collected all sequences through low-speed teleoperation to limit motion blur and manually inspected the RGB images to remove blurred frames. The dataset contains 71,536 RGB images at 2880 × 1860 2880\times 1860 resolution and 35,770 LiDAR frames, together with synchronized IMU measurements, spanning 59.6 minutes and approximately 1.15 km. Individual sequences range from 1.77 to 11.11 minutes, with trajectories approaching 200 m. Table 6 reports per-sequence statistics, with sequence names matching the benchmark evaluation. sections.heading: A.5 Implementation and Evaluation Protocols
sections.text: Implementation. All experiments use NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPUs. LiDAR–inertial bundle adjustment uses a ten-scan sliding window. Gaussian refinement runs for 15,000 steps with camera poses and exposure transforms fixed, following the repair schedule in Appendix A.3.2 . Offline 3DGS baselines are trained for 30,000 steps. Evaluation protocols. Trajectory evaluation reports translational ATE RMSE after SE(3) alignment for metric methods and Sim(3) alignment for vision-only methods. Each trajectory is evaluated at timestamps with valid reference associations. Reported means weight sequences equally. Pose-stage comparisons use matched timestamps within each run; offline HBA results are reported separately rather than treated as a paired stage ablation. Rendering evaluation holds out every eighth image from Gaussian optimization. On Oxford Spires, M2DGR, and INS, offline 3DGS uses fixed MIRAGE online poses. MIRAGE rendering results use the Gaussian maps after refinement, without HBA pose updates; Gaussian-LIC2 results use its online maps. Comparisons exclude Observatory 02, Church 03, and indoor_sq2 because Gaussian-LIC2 did not complete reconstruction. On the MIRAGE benchmark, visual baselines use one-in-twelve sampling of the same preprocessed RGB sequences, without LiDAR, IMU, or reference-pose inputs. Each method supplies only its predicted poses to downstream 3DGS. These poses remain fixed during training, and Gaussians are initialized from training-view correspondences using a common triangulation procedure. The common-frame evaluation uses shared training and test images. MASt3R-SLAM is evaluated on registered keyframes, and its rendering results are excluded from common-frame rankings. Ours (reference) uses the same 3DGS procedure with MIRAGE reference poses. Stream PSNR reports the complete MIRAGE pipeline after refinement on its own held-out images, rather than the shared stride-12 test set. For the visual ablation, camera poses are obtained by interpolating LiDAR–inertial poses to image timestamps and applying calibrated extrinsics; RGB supervision for Gaussian reconstruction is retained. Photometric and geometry-aware refinement start from the same streaming map and share the optimization budget, fixed poses and exposure, renderer, and test views. Photometric refinement uses only ℒ 1 \mathcal{L}_{1} and SSIM losses with a fixed primitive count.

sections.heading: A.7 Limitations
sections.text: While MIRAGE achieves accurate metric pose estimation and high-fidelity reconstruction, several limitations remain. First, our benchmark focuses on static indoor scenes and does not assess the impact of dynamic objects on localization and reconstruction. Second, our data acquisition and reconstruction pipelines lack dedicated treatment of transparent and semi-transparent objects, which can compromise geometric accuracy and rendering quality. These limitations motivate future work on extending the benchmark to dynamic scenes and improving reconstruction of challenging materials.

Project Page: MIRAGE-URL . 1 Introduction Recent advances in 3D scene representation and camera pose estimation have substantially improved the quality and practicality of image-based reconstruction. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) ( Kerbl et al., 2023 ) represents scenes with optimizable anisotropic Gaussian primitives and an efficient differentiable rasterizer, enabling high-fidelity real-time novel-view synthesis. In parallel, feed-forward geometric models ( Leroy et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025a ; Wang et al., 2025b ) have made substantial progress in jointly inferring camera poses and scene geometry from unposed images. These advances have further driven the development of increasingly capable online tracking, mapping, and on-the-fly reconstruction systems ( Matsuki et al., 2024 ; Huang et al., 2024 ; Keetha et al., 2024 ; Meuleman et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2025 ) . More recent methods combine SLAM frameworks with data-driven feed-forward priors to further improve pose estimation and reconstruction quality in streaming scenarios ( Li et al., 2026b ; Ren et al., 2026 ) . However, purely visual reconstruction remains subject to global similarity ambiguity, while accumulated errors in learned geometry and pose estimation can lead to scale and motion drift over long sequences. These limitations highlight the need for an explicit metric anchor to achieve both high-fidelity reconstruction and a physically grounded trajectory. LiDAR–IMU sensing provides the metric scale and motion constraints missing from purely visual reconstruction. However, simply introducing a metric anchor does not resolve how feed-forward visual geometry should influence online pose refinement. Visual priors can improve local alignment and reconstruction quality, yet unreliable corrections may compromise metric consistency, while overly suppressing them can forfeit useful image-space refinement. Since the reliability of visual corrections varies with correspondence support and cross-modal agreement, a fixed fusion strategy is insufficient. The key challenge is therefore to selectively exploit feed-forward visual geometry while preserving a metrically consistent trajectory. We propose MIRAGE 1 1 1 The name reflects the gap between visual plausibility and metric consistency. , an on-the-fly reconstruction framework that combines feed-forward visual geometry with LiDAR–IMU sensing to jointly achieve metrically accurate pose estimation and high-fidelity Gaussian reconstruction. MIRAGE uses LiDAR–IMU motion as a metric anchor and selectively incorporates visual pose corrections according to correspondence support and cross-modal agreement, retaining useful visual refinement without compromising metric consistency. Given the stabilized metric trajectory, MIRAGE further leverages image residuals and LiDAR geometry for structure-aware Gaussian refinement, improving reconstruction quality while keeping the camera poses fixed. Experiments on Oxford Spires ( Tao et al., 2026 ) , M2DGR ( Yin et al., 2022 ) and INS ( Deng et al., 2025a ) demonstrate that MIRAGE achieves accurate and metrically consistent trajectory estimation while maintaining high-fidelity, photorealistic Gaussian reconstruction. Notably, MIRAGE achieves higher trajectory accuracy than COLMAP, despite COLMAP being a computationally expensive method widely used to establish reference trajectories for vision-only benchmarks. This demonstrates MIRAGE’s potential to provide reliable reference trajectories for benchmarking vision-only reconstruction methods. Long-horizon benchmarks for monocular reconstruction in large-scale indoor environments remain limited. To fill this gap, we develop a remotely operated capture platform with hardware-synchronized cameras, LiDAR, and IMU, and collect ten long-horizon sequences across diverse indoor scenes, as shown in Figure 1 . MIRAGE is then used to establish accurate 6-DoF reference trajectories for these sequences, forming a vision-only benchmark for large-scale indoor reconstruction. We further evaluate recent long-horizon monocular reconstruction methods on this benchmark. Our contributions are threefold: • Reliability-gated metric trajectory inference. We anchor feed-forward visual geometry to LiDAR–IMU metric motion and treat visual pose updates as correction proposals, selectively committing them according to correspondence support and cross-modal consistency to improve image-space alignment without compromising metric trajectory accuracy. • Pose-fixed structure-aware Gaussian refinement. We decouple scene refinement from trajectory estimation by fixing the metric camera poses and using image residuals together with LiDAR depth evidence to diagnose and repair oversized, misplaced, and missing primitives, improving geometric detail and appearance without perturbing the recovered trajectory. • A long-horizon benchmark dataset for real-world indoor reconstruction. We introduce a large-scale indoor benchmark comprising 10 synchronized RGB–LiDAR–IMU sequences, with 71,536 RGB frames spanning 59.6 minutes and 1.15 km across laboratories, dining areas, offices, and long corridors. The benchmark provides full 6-DoF reference trajectories and supports joint evaluation of long-horizon metric localization and high-fidelity 3D reconstruction. 2 Related Work 2.1 Visual Pose Estimation and Streaming Gaussian Reconstruction Learned geometry models ( Wang et al., 2024 ; Leroy et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025a ; Lin et al., 2025b ) provide dense priors for pose estimation and reconstruction. Recent methods incorporate these priors into visual tracking and global optimization ( Murai et al., 2025 ; Maggio et al., 2026 ; Maggio and Carlone, 2026 ) , exploit geometric context for reconstruction ( Chen et al., 2026 ; Xie et al., 2026 ) , or combine feed-forward predictions with global structure-from-motion optimization ( Deng et al., 2026 ; Pan et al., 2026 ) . Gaussian SLAM ( Matsuki et al., 2024 ; Huang et al., 2024 ; Keetha et al., 2024 ) extends 3DGS ( Kerbl et al., 2023 ) to incremental tracking and mapping. Other approaches predict Gaussians from image streams ( Chen et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2025 ) , optimize scenes incrementally ( Meuleman et al., 2025 ; Meuleman et al., 2026 ) , or combine learned priors with online pose and map optimization ( Lin et al., 2025a ; Li et al., 2026b ; Jiang et al., 2026 ; Ren et al., 2026 ) . Monocular reconstruction nevertheless remains scale-ambiguous, and learned priors do not guarantee metric accuracy or drift-free trajectories over long traversals. 2.2 LiDAR–Inertial Estimation and Multimodal Gaussian Mapping LiDAR–inertial estimators ( Shan et al., 2020 ; Xu et al., 2022 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) recover metric motion from range and inertial constraints, while visual–LiDAR systems ( Shan et al., 2021 ; Lin and Zhang, 2022 ; Zheng et al., 2022 ; Zheng et al., 2025 ; Zhao et al., 2025 ) incorporate image observations. Multimodal Gaussian mapping ( Hong et al., 2024 ; Lang et al., 2025 ; Xie et al., 2025 ; Jiang et al., 2024 ; Deng et al., 2025b ; Cui et al., 2024 ) uses metric poses and LiDAR geometry for initialization and photometric refinement. Recent methods further incorporate Gaussian-map observations into localization ( Hong et al., 2025 ; Lang et al., 2026 ) or feed-forward priors into estimation and mapping ( Wang et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026a ) . MIRAGE regulates pose corrections using visual and geometric evidence to support both metric accuracy and rendering quality. 2.3 Benchmarks for Multimodal Localization and Reconstruction Visual benchmarks ( Sturm et al., 2012 ; Dai et al., 2017 ; Knapitsch et al., 2017 ) support tracking or reconstruction evaluation without mobile 3D LiDAR streams. ScanNet++ ( Yeshwanth et al., 2023 ) combines high-resolution RGB, surveyed laser geometry, and mobile RGB-D/IMU data. Mobile datasets vary in sensing and supervision: MulRan ( Kim et al., 2020 ) lacks camera images, Hilti-Oxford ( Zhang et al., 2023 ) uses grayscale cameras, and FAST-LIVO2’s self-collected sequences ( Zheng et al., 2025 ) lack pose ground truth. RGB–LiDAR–IMU datasets ( Tao et al., 2026 ; Yin et al., 2022 ; Jiao et al., 2022 ; Wei et al., 2025 ; Zhao et al., 2024 ) cover diverse environments and platforms, while recent multimodal benchmarks ( Deng et al., 2025a ; Lang et al., 2026 ) provide reference geometry and poses for localization and rendering evaluation. Nevertheless, synchronized RGB–LiDAR–IMU benchmarks with full 6-DoF reference trajectories over long, object-rich indoor traversals remain scarce. Our extended captures in laboratories, offices, and dining spaces address this gap, supporting joint evaluation of trajectory accuracy and downstream Gaussian reconstruction. 3 Method 3.1 Overview Figure 2: Pipeline of MIRAGE. We anchor feed-forward visual geometry to LiDAR–IMU motion for metric pose estimation and streaming Gaussian mapping. Local metric constraints support visual pose refinement, while reliability-aware loop correction controls correction magnitude and selectively applies rotation to balance revisit alignment and local motion consistency. The resulting poses drive a triangle-associated Gaussian map. With poses fixed, offline geometry-aware refinement improves scene structure using image residuals and LiDAR support. Figure 2 summarizes MIRAGE. Given synchronized RGB, LiDAR, and IMU streams, we anchor feed-forward visual geometry to LiDAR–IMU motion for metric camera pose estimation. Correspondence support and cross-modal agreement regulate pose corrections (Section 3.2 ). The resulting poses drive streaming Gaussian reconstruction. After streaming, we fix camera poses and refine the Gaussian map offline, using image residuals and LiDAR depth to guide primitive splitting, replacement, and insertion (Section 3.3 ). We also introduce a synchronized multimodal indoor benchmark with MIRAGE-derived 6-DoF reference trajectories for evaluating long-horizon monocular reconstruction (Section 3.4 ). 3.2 Pose Estimation We anchor visual pose estimation to LiDAR–IMU motion through a local-to-global pipeline. Tracking combines dense visual correspondences with LiDAR-derived metric depth to estimate frame-to-keyframe poses (Section 3.2.1 ). Local optimization refines keyframe poses using visual consistency constraints and metric position anchors (Section 3.2.2 ). Loop closure selectively corrects these anchors, and global trajectory fusion combines them with local visual motion to produce per-image camera poses (Section 3.2.3 ). 3.2.1 Metric-Guided Visual Tracking For the current frame f f and reference keyframe k k , we estimate the frame-to-keyframe transformation 𝐓 k ​ f V = ( 𝐓 k V ) − 1 ​ 𝐓 f V \mathbf{T}_{kf}^{\mathrm{V}}=(\mathbf{T}_{k}^{\mathrm{V}})^{-1}\mathbf{T}_{f}^{\mathrm{V}} , where 𝐓 f V , 𝐓 k V ∈ SE ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathbf{T}_{f}^{\mathrm{V}},\mathbf{T}_{k}^{\mathrm{V}}\in\mathrm{SE}(3) are their visual camera-to-world poses. Observation-supported loop correction. We generate initial loop candidates following ( Liu et al., 2026 ) and rigidly align the resulting pose-graph optimization (PGO) proposals to the current metric trajectory without scale fitting. We assess each proposal from two complementary perspectives: (1) geometric consistency , evaluating improvements in revisit alignment and the risk of disrupting local structure; and (2) visual consistency , evaluating reprojection agreement with available image correspondences. These cues determine the accepted correction magnitude. Rotation updates are gated separately and require additional geometric benefit relative to their risk; otherwise, the current metric orientations are retained, as shown in Figure 2 . Accepted corrections update the metric anchors and propagate to subsequent metric poses. Details are provided in Appendix A.2.3 . Metric-anchored visual motion fusion. We interpolate consecutive metric anchors to obtain a baseline camera trajectory. We then incorporate visual motion between these anchors, using the deviation of the visual trajectory from the interpolation of its poses at the same two anchor timestamps. (2) The fused trajectory matches the metric anchors exactly while retaining visual motion residuals between them. Details are provided in Appendix A.2.4 . We optionally refine the accepted metric trajectory offline using hierarchical LiDAR bundle adjustment ( Liu et al., 2023 ) , exporting a separate trajectory as described in Appendix A.2.5 . 3.3 Geometry-Aware Gaussian Reconstruction We reconstruct scenes using LiDAR to constrain geometry and RGB images to supervise appearance. Inspired by PLANING ( Jiang et al., 2026 ) , we use a triangle–Gaussian representation that couples explicit surface geometry with Gaussian appearance. Streaming Gaussian reconstruction. For each incoming keyframe, we initialize triangle geometry from LiDAR depth and normals, and Gaussian appearance from RGB observations. We then jointly optimize geometry and appearance through differentiable rendering: depth and normal consistency constrain geometry, while photometric losses supervise appearance. When camera poses are updated, we transform the associated primitives accordingly to maintain map consistency. Details are provided in Appendix A.3 . Geometry-aware Gaussian refinement. Following prior work ( Li et al., 2026b ; Meuleman et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) , we refine the streamed scene offline to improve global scene consistency and reconstruction accuracy. With camera poses fixed, LiDAR depth constrains geometry, while RGB images refine appearance. During refinement, we periodically diagnose and repair regions with high rendering error using motion-compensated LiDAR depth and multi-view consistency checks. (1) Oversized Gaussians whose depths agree with LiDAR measurements but fail to resolve image detail are split into smaller primitives. (2) Gaussians with persistent depth disagreement are replaced with primitives reinitialized using LiDAR depth and local normals. (3) At locations with valid LiDAR depth but insufficient Gaussian coverage, we insert new primitives using depth for position, local normals for orientation, and RGB observations for color. Alongside the photometric loss, we apply a point-to-plane penalty constructed from LiDAR depth and local normals to newly created or reinitialized Gaussians, penalizing position errors along the normal direction while allowing tangential adjustment. Repair criteria and loss details are provided in Appendix A.3.2 . 3.4 A Benchmark for Long-Horizon Indoor Reconstruction We introduce a benchmark for long-horizon monocular streaming reconstruction. Our platform (Fig. 1 , right) integrates a wide-angle RGB camera, two LiDARs, and one LiDAR’s built-in IMU. The dual-LiDAR configuration combines broad coverage for robust localization with dense sampling for detailed reconstruction. Custom hardware synchronization and calibrated extrinsics align the sensor streams. We collected sequences through low-speed teleoperation to limit motion blur and removed blurred images through manual inspection. The dataset comprises 10 sequences across four categories: laboratories and dining areas with numerous objects and reflective surfaces, an office, and long, low-texture corridors that challenge visual tracking. It contains 71,536 RGB images at 2880 × 1860 2880\times 1860 resolution, spanning 59.6 minutes and 1.15 km, with trajectories approaching 200 m. We provide synchronized RGB–LiDAR–IMU data, sensor intrinsics and extrinsics, global LiDAR reference point clouds, and MIRAGE-derived 6-DoF reference poses. MIRAGE’s trajectory accuracy is validated on Oxford Spires ( Tao et al., 2026 ) and M2DGR ( Yin et al., 2022 ) . Platform details and dataset statistics appear in Appendix A.4 . We evaluate RGB-only methods on global trajectory accuracy and downstream reconstruction quality. We report absolute trajectory error (ATE) RMSE after Sim(3) alignment to the reference poses. For reconstruction evaluation, we train standard 3DGS ( Kerbl et al., 2023 ) with each method’s predicted poses held fixed. Held-out novel view synthesis (NVS) PSNR serves as a downstream indicator of local multi-view pose consistency. 4 Experiments 4.1 Experimental Setup Datasets and Metrics. We evaluate MIRAGE on Oxford Spires ( Tao et al., 2026 ) , M2DGR ( Yin et al., 2022 ) , and INS ( Deng et al., 2025a ) , reporting absolute trajectory error (ATE) RMSE for trajectory accuracy and PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS ( Zhang et al., 2018 ) for rendering quality. We additionally evaluate representative vision-only methods on our proposed MIRAGE benchmark, reporting ATE RMSE after Sim(3) alignment to the reference trajectories we provide. Details are provided in Appendix A.5 . Baselines. On Oxford Spires, M2DGR, and INS, our comparisons include LiDAR–inertial odometry (EllipseLIO ( Border and Chli, 2026 ) ), LiDAR–inertial–visual odometry (Fast-LIVO2 ( Zheng et al., 2025 ) ), LiDAR–inertial SLAM without visual input (Fast-LIO-SLAM and Voxel-SLAM ( Liu et al., 2026 ) ), and vision-only methods (LingBot-Map ( Chen et al., 2026 ) , GLUEMAP ( Pan et al., 2026 ) , and COLMAP ( Schönberger and Frahm, 2016 ) ). We also compare with Gaussian-LIC2 ( Lang et al., 2026 ) , a tightly coupled LiDAR–inertial–visual Gaussian SLAM system. On our MIRAGE benchmark, we evaluate recent strong vision-only methods, including LingBot-Map, GLUEMAP, LoGeR ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) , Scal3R ( Xie et al., 2026 ) , and ABot-Recon ( Han et al., 2026 ) , alongside MASt3R-SLAM ( Murai et al., 2025 ) . Implementation Details. Following the 3DGS evaluation protocol ( Kerbl et al., 2023 ) , we hold out every eighth image for rendering evaluation. LiDAR–inertial local bundle adjustment uses a ten-scan sliding window. Gaussian refinement runs for 15,000 steps with camera poses and exposure transforms fixed, performing splitting every 1,000 steps from step 2,000 through 8,000. All experiments are conducted on NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPUs. 4.2 Trajectory Accuracy MIRAGE completes all 15 sequences and achieves the lowest reported online ATE on 12 while maintaining a moderate latency of 0.73 s/frame (Table 1 ). Averaged equally across sequences, its ATE is 4.22 cm versus 7.49 cm for EllipseLIO, a 43.7% reduction. On large-scale Oxford Spires traversals and low-texture INS scenes, LingBot-Map exhibits substantial trajectory errors, while Fast-LIVO2 and Gaussian-LIC2 show severe errors or failures in our reproductions. MIRAGE maintains ATE below 10 cm on every sequence. These results are consistent with its reliability-aware design: metric anchors constrain drift, while correspondence support and cross-modal agreement regulate visual corrections to exploit useful evidence and limit unreliable updates. Visual and geometric evidence guide trajectory corrections, while LiDAR depth and image residuals drive Gaussian repair with camera poses fixed. Experiments on Oxford Spires, M2DGR, and INS demonstrate accurate trajectories and high-fidelity rendering.
